doc.title: Jerry Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe and Christian Goodwillie, via Zoom, June 30, 2021

chapter: Pharaoh Sanders and the Theresa catalog
title: Allen Pittman and the Theresa Records catalog
summary: Gordon met Allen Pittman at the NAIRD convention; Pittman's Theresa label put out Pharaoh Sanders and John Hicks, and sold the label to Gordon.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: All right. So there used to be a record convention in Philadelphia. The name of the organization was NAIRD — N-A-I-R-D. National Association of Independent Record Distributors, and kind of at the center of that organization was Richmond Brothers which was a one-stop in the Philadelphia area. And so once a year, you know Indy record label owners would come into Philly and they would all come to my store, all of them, and look to see if I was carrying their records. It was really fun to see, you know, they would look, sometimes they would introduce themselves, sometimes they would — and I became friends with a guy, we really got along great and we became friends, and his name was Allen Pittman. And this guy was a very very non-religious, but he was a saint typical of many of the people in jazz as to like making great sacrifices in an unsustainable business in the service of jazz, one of them was Allen Pittman. He was a doctor, not a medical doctor but he worked for the FDA and I think that’s the case, I’m not positive. And made good money during the day and flushing it away at night starting a jazz label, which he was motivated to do. And his wife hated it because he was always running around, he bought a van, he signed artists, he started taking all the artists to their gigs, carrying their amplifiers and putting them in his van and doing all this crazy stuff, and the wife could not relate to it. And Allen even, Dr. Pittman, and Pharaoh did a song called Dr. Pitt, P-I-T-T. His wife hated this whole thing and was crazy, and he named the label after her to pacify her, so that he named it Theresa Records. But they got divorced quickly anyway, it didn’t take long, but the name stayed. And he was in the Bay area and he started signing his friends. He was an avid concert goer, he was a musician, very very very cool guy. And he had signed Pharaoh, John Hicks, and other — Bobby Hutcherson for one album, other musicians in the Bay area. And he, the records Sun Ra had some people might say, not all people, some people would say Sun Ra’s records on Impulse — at the end of his Impulse deal and during the Arista had declined, they were not the great, the “Creator has a Master Plan,” “Karma,” “Jewels of Thought,” you know, some people might think the records had declined a little bit. And Allen Pittman brought him back.

Allen Pittman put out, on his Theresa label, two of the great Pharaoh albums ever. Despite that, and he had put out more than two, but there were two two-record sets that he put out that became classics in jazz and for Pharaoh Sanders. And despite that and putting out a series of great albums, he couldn’t take it anymore, losing money, getting screwed around by distributors, that kind of stuff. And Allen was a peaceful man. He was not the guy to collect money. “Give me my money or else,” that was not Allen Pittman. He was a sweet, soft guy. And then one day I get a call from Allen out of the blue and I only knew him from visiting the store during the NAIRD convention and he said, “Jerry I can’t take it anymore I want to sell the record label.” So he told me this is what I want, I don’t want to negotiate it, this is what I want, you know, I’d like to sell you the whole record label and I think he thought that you know I would do his artists justice and his creations justice and all that. So he introduced me to the artists, he invited Pharaoh over to his place to meet me and I got to meet Pharaoh and I did several times. He was a great guy. And I owe Allen Pittman a lot. The Theresa catalog was magnificent, I put out a lot of good records, a lot of John Hicks records also that were great, important John Hicks records. So Christian that’s my Pharaoh Sanders story.
No that’s great, I mean I completely agree with you on the arc of the recordings there in terms of him kind of coming back into his own a bit at that time.
